title: 6 improvements that make Grafana Assistant better at helping your workflows
summary:
When you ask Grafana Assistant to build a dashboard or investigate an alert, you're doing so because there's work to be done. To do that work effectively, you need the right data, changes you can inspect, and conclusions supported by evidence. You also want Assistant to avoid mistakes and act quickly.

Over the past six months, our team has worked hard to improve what makes those outcomes possible. We’ve changed how agents find context, discover capabilities, edit dashboards, and recover from errors. At the same time, we’ve built better ways to determine whether an improvement actually helps.

These projects are closely connected. Better evaluations reveal where an agent struggles. Those findings guide changes to its tools and context. Production telemetry tells us whether those changes worked and where to look next.

We've been documenting this work on our engineering blog, Unprompted, taking deep dives into the decisions and implementations that went into those efforts. Today, I want to share how those changes have translated to better outcomes for our users.

Dashboarding: faster, prettier, less errors

By mid-2026, dashboarding mode accounted for 27% of Assistant conversations. Users were also telling us exactly where it needed to work better: some operations were slow, consumed too many tokens, or changed things they should have left alone.

The team started by establishing a baseline with Agent Observability and building reproducible tests. Over roughly 10 weeks, the reported dashboarding error rate fell from 2.47% to 0.65%. The 95th-percentile latency for individual operations dropped from 63 seconds to 28.8 seconds, while cost per request fell by 18%.

As Dominik Broj describes in his dashboarding write-up, those results came from repeated, specific improvements. Engineers found failures in production, reproduced them as evaluation scenarios, fixed the underlying problems, and checked the results after rollout. The dashboarding test catalog grew from 78 scenarios to nearly 200.

Learn more: Read Dominik's blog post, "Our journey to improve Grafana Assistant dashboarding mode"

Others build agent loops, we build evaluation loops to get you the best outcomes

That process matters beyond dashboarding. It gives us a way to turn individual reports into improvements that can be tested again whenever the system changes.

An AI agent can produce a convincing response even when its underlying work is wrong. A panel might render successfully while showing the wrong aggregation. An investigation might identify a plausible cause without enough evidence. Evaluating the final answer alone misses much of what determines whether the task succeeded.

In his blog post about building an evaluation loop for Assistant, Yasir Ekinci explains how we separate the behavior we want from the prompts and code that implement it. Scenarios define realistic tasks and success criteria. Graders examine queries, tool calls, saved state, and conclusions. Repeated runs expose inconsistent behavior, and comparisons track quality alongside cost and latency.

That separation gives us room to experiment. We can change a prompt, tool, or model while checking against the same expectations. Coding agents also help inspect failures and propose changes, which go back through the evaluation loop for verification and human review.

Learn more: Read Yasir's blog post, "Building an evaluation loop for Grafana Assistant"

gcx: teaching your local agent how to designing a CLI built for agents

This same principle appears in Ward Bekker’s account of designing gcx. Watching agents use our CLI revealed repeated failures: guessing flags, retrying unsuccessful commands, and requesting far more output than they needed.

The fixes that came with gcx, our CLI designed specifically for agents, which made the interface more informative. Commands describe their capabilities. Errors explain how to recover. Agents can inspect available fields and filter results before bringing them into context. Knowledge that once required a separate playbook increasingly lives in the tool itself, where it can stay aligned with the implementation.

At its core, gcx asks one practical question: what should the interface tell the agent so it can take the next step correctly?

Lowering the context burden

That question becomes more important as the number of capabilities grows. In his post on progressive tool discovery, Cyril Tovena describes how Assistant discovers detailed tool instructions when it needs them. Instead of loading every schema upfront, it starts with compact entry points and retrieves the relevant manual.

Across the full registered tool surface measured in the post, initial tool definitions shrank from roughly 54,500 estimated tokens to 504. That is a 99.1% reduction in that specific context overhead; actual session savings depend on the capabilities available and used.

The broader benefit is that Assistant can gain capabilities without every conversation carrying all their instructions and that your usage gets cheaper: less tokens in the system prompt, less tax upfront. We still measure the complete workflow: smaller prompts are only helpful if discovery does not introduce excessive steps or delays.

Learn more: Read Ward's blog post, "CLIs in the age of agents: how we designed gcx," and Cyril's blog post, "Progressive tool discovery: battling tool overload in AI agents"

Finding stuff doesn’t need to be hard

Your dashboards, alerts, and incident histories contain knowledge about how your systems work. Making that knowledge accessible requires more than placing documents in a search index.

Ioanna Armouti’s story about improving Assitant's search capabilities describes the decisions behind its retrieval system. For dashboards, embedding raw panel JSON drew attention toward rendering details. Representing a panel through its folder, dashboard, row, description, and queries made its purpose clearer. Incident summaries needed different treatment from noisy activity feeds. Permissions needed checking when results were retrieved, because access can change after indexing.

There is a connection here to tool discovery and dashboard editing: all three make relevant information easier to reach while controlling how much enters the agent’s context. More available information helps only when the agent can find and use the right portion.

The investigation team saw that directly when testing against real incidents.

Learn more: Read Ioanna's blog post, "Search, but deeper: how Grafana Assistant finds the right context"

Faster and better root causes with Investigations

Earlier this year we realized that successful tests on synthetic telemetry were insufficient. Real incidents brought incomplete data, competing explanations, and distracting signals.

In his post, William Dumont describes how we borrowed a concept from the world of competitive programming to compare agent variants on resolved incidents and how that exposed concrete problems.

One agent inferred too much from an alert’s name; fetching the actual alert definition gave it a better starting point. Another avoided a useful tool because its instructions described the wrong query language; filtering retrieved background information reduced irrelevant context.

Scores on the internal difficult-incident suite moved from 52% to 69% during a week of iteration. That score measures performance on those benchmark cases. The lasting value is the ability to identify why one investigation succeeds where another struggles—and to keep testing the difficult behavior of acknowledging insufficient evidence. Ultimately, this work, which is ongoing, translates to more reliable recommendations, which builds better trust and leads to better outcomes.

Learn more: Read William's blog post, "Enter the arena: evaluating and improving Grafana Assistant Investigations against real incidents"

Evaluations at scale don’t need to be expensive

As agents began doing longer sequences of work, our original production evaluator increasingly missed failures because it focused too heavily on response text. Yasir Ekinci and Sven Großmann describe the rebuild: show the evaluator more of the agent’s work, let it recognize partial completion, and test its judgments against a stronger reference reviewer.

They then tested Jev, a model designed for structured decisions. It was substantially faster and cheaper, but agreed with the reference reviewer much less well than the strongest generative judge. We retained the stronger judge for the main quality score and introduced Jev as an optional provider with a trace-triage template. Its suitability for that different task still requires representative validation.

That is an important part of experimentation: understanding where a new approach fits, including where the evidence says to keep what already works.

These projects also explain the relationship between Grafana Assistant and Agent Observability. Building and operating Assistant gives us difficult, practical questions about agent behavior. Agent Observability helps us answer them through traces, evaluations, and comparisons—and makes those capabilities available to customers building agents of their own.

Learn more: Read Sven and Yasir's blog post, "Judge Jev: Can a typed-decision model grade your agent?"

Redefining how we work so we can deliver better products quicker

In my post about how we build AI at Grafana Labs, I described our approach as small, meaningful iterations grounded in customer problems. We take the customer problems and try to solve them. Along the way, some things work (that’s the blog post you can read!), some things don’t work—and that’s okay. We want to move quickly, which means we empower everyone to experiment quickly in any direction.

Learn more: Read my blog post, "How we build AI at Grafana Labs: small steps that add up to actually useful AI"

This week at ObservabilityCon 2026, we’ll take all this one step further, highlighting our continued efforts to deliver AI capabilities that help you work smarter and faster. Be sure to register for the in-person event or watch our keynote livestream.

title: Get observability in your pocket with the Grafana mobile app
summary:
When you’re on the go, your phone is often the only observability tool you have. And what you can do with it in the first few minutes matters. 

With the incredible innovation that has gone into mobile CPUs, GPUs and displays, a phone is a powerful device where you can immediately see what’s happening and start acting on it. And the Grafana mobile app now allows you to both see and act. 

The app (available for Android and iOS) has always been good at notifying you of what's happening—alerts, incidents, and on-call schedules, previously under the Grafana IRM name. Now you can also ask questions in natural language, view your dashboards, and take actions across your stack. It is not a smaller, more cramped version of your computer, but a powerful starting point for the first few minutes of an incident. 

Grafana Assistant on your phone

Grafana Assistant is a context-aware agent that can answer questions and take action across your stack. It already lives where you work: as a sidebar chat in the Grafana web UI, in Workspace if you prefer a conversation-focused experience for Grafana, in Slack or Microsoft Teams, or through gcx on the command line. It now runs on your phone, too, with the same conversations and the same abilities. 

What makes Assistant useful is that it never starts from zero. It knows which stack you're in, which dashboard or alert you're looking at, and how your data is shaped. 

With Assistant on your phone, you can:

  • Understand alerts and incidents: Catch up on what’s happened, explore what changed, and check whether a problem has occurred before.

  • Find relevant dashboards: Ask which dashboards can help you understand an issue and open them right from the conversation.

  • Check your on-call schedule: Find out when you’re on rotation without hunting through schedules.

  • Launch an investigation: Get Assistant working on a complex issue before you reach your laptop.

  • Pick up where you left off: Continue the same conversation on your computer, with the context intact.

Getting started takes just a question. For example, when an alert fires, you can open Assistant directly from it. The alert context is automatically included in the conversation, so you can immediately ask: 

Incidents work the same way, with the conversation pre-seeded with the incident context:

Follow-up questions stay in the same context, so you can narrow down without repeating yourself: 

Assistant can recommend an existing dashboard based on the conversation, allowing you to see it right away. Or you can easily ask:

And when you get back to your computer, you can continue the same conversation without losing any context:

Incident response on the go

Incident response is core to how effective engineering teams work. The app allows you to see alert groups, incidents, and on-call schedules:

You can also see the timeline of an incident, who was paged, and any other details:

If you use several devices, you can choose which of them gets paged in the notifications settings:

The app can answer less pressing questions, too. If you’re thinking about a weekend away at the end of the month and want to know whether you’re on the rotation before you commit, that’s a question Assistant can easily answer:

And when the issue seems complex, you can ask Assistant to kick off an investigation right from your phone. By the time you get to your laptop, there's a report waiting: the hypotheses it pursued, how each one was validated or ruled out, and where that trail led. 

Your dashboards, wherever you are

Dashboards are the workhorses of Grafana. They're what most people open first in the morning, what's on the screen mounted on the office wall, and what a team builds over years as it learns what actually matters about its systems. Those same dashboards now open on your phone. They reflow to fit a small screen, and the ones you've starred come first:

Most dashboard use is a glance. You may have shipped a deploy, and on the train ride home you need to check that the error rate is flat. That's a perfect use case for a phone:

Have a key metric that you want to check regularly? You can add any panel to the app’s home tab showing your preferred data and time frame right after opening the app:

A different way of working, not a smaller one

None of this makes the phone a replacement for a real workstation. If you're trying to correlate five signals across three services to track down a root cause, you want a big screen, a keyboard, and four tabs open. That's not changing, and it shouldn't. 

But the Grafana mobile app gives us a different way of working. Your first question gets asked in a queue for coffee. An investigation is launched from the back of a taxi. More context to understand an issue is gathered while you wait for a train. And the resulting conversations, investigations, dashboards, or acknowledgements are waiting in the Grafana web UI when you finally reach your computer, so that you could continue rather than opening it cold. 

The rename from Grafana IRM to the Grafana app is a statement of direction. In addition to integrating Assistant and dashboards, more of Grafana is on the way as the app grows beyond its IRM roots. What we're building toward is a real window into your stack that happens to live in your pocket.

title: Coverage-first or cost-first: two ways to automatically apply Adaptive Metrics' recommendations
summary:
Adaptive Metrics , which is part of the Adaptive Telemetry suite, looks at how your metrics are actually used and recommends how much detail you should keep for each metric. This helps you cut costs while still retaining the data you actually need. 

Last year we added auto-apply capabilities that let you implement those recommendations automatically, but only with coverage-first behavior, maximizing coverage of whatever you're querying. If your team wanted anything different, the only option was to review and apply recommendations by hand. 

But now, with the General Availability release of auto-apply, we've added a second mode: cost-first, a built-in safeguard that only applies recommendations that won't increase your total active series—ensuring optimization never turns into a cost spike. 

Auto-Apply continuously applies recommendations in either mode with no human intervention, while your existing dashboards, alerts, and queries keep working unchanged.

How cost-first mode decides what to apply

Every recommendation Adaptive Metrics generates comes with a projected change to your series count—some recommendations decrease it, others increase it. Cost-first mode can now take those projected changes into account, much like a careful manual review would, in three steps:

  1. Series-reducing recommendations always apply. Anything that lowers your projected series count goes through immediately, including brand-new recommendations.

  2. Series-increasing recommendations get ranked. Anything that would raise your projected series count is sorted from least impactful to most impactful.

  3. Adaptive Metrics stops at your current total. It works down that ranked list, applying recommendations until the next one would push your projected series count above where it started the cycle.

How coverage-first mode decides what to apply

Coverage-first works more simply than cost-first does: every recommendation gets applied as soon as it's generated, whether it lowers your series count or raises it.

  1. Every recommendation applies, no ranking required. Coverage-first doesn't weigh one recommendation against another or check a budget. It just applies what Adaptive Metrics finds.

  2. Increases go through immediately. If a query comes in for data that's already been aggregated away, the recommendation to restore it at full resolution applies right away, because someone clearly needs that data.

  3. Your metrics stay in lockstep with usage. As what you query shifts week to week, coverage-first adjusts automatically, so nothing you actually use ever falls out of resolution.

The tradeoff is the one cost-first exists to solve: because every increasing recommendation applies too, a spike in queries against previously-aggregated data shows up as a spike in series count.

A simplified example makes this concrete. Say a cycle generates three recommendations:

Recommendation

Effect on series count

Cost-first applied?

Coverage-first applied?

Why

1

-10

Yes

Yes

Decreases series count

2

+5

Yes

Yes

Running total still at or below where it started

3

+10

No

Yes

Would push the running total above where it started

The net effect is that your series count stays flat or drops. It never rises above where you started the cycle, which is the guarantee cost-first mode is built around.

Cost-first vs. coverage-first: when to apply each one

Adaptive Metrics' original auto-apply behavior, coverage-first, maximizes coverage of whatever you're actually querying. It's still there, and it's still the better fit for some of your data. If a dataset is business critical and your team knows exactly what it's querying and why, you want nothing standing between a real query and the raw data behind it. That's the mode we at Grafana Labs use internally for our own critical telemetry.

Cost-first mode is the better fit where cost matters more than guaranteed full coverage. For example, it would be well suited for a PromptQL query that asks for more than the person writing it realized, or an agent issuing queries on your behalf with no visibility into the cost impact downstream. That's increasingly common as less experienced users get access to larger datasets without realizing the potential impact of their queries. In those cases, you'd rather have Adaptive Metrics hold the line on cost and let you review and restore specific data later than have it de-aggregate automatically every time something gets queried unintentionally.

You also don't have to pick one mode for all of your data. Adaptive Metrics' segments feature lets you partition your telemetry along a dimension you choose (e.g., by team, environment, or cluster) and set a different mode on each segment independently. Keep coverage-first on the segments your experts own, and turn on cost-first mode for the segments where cost predictability matters more. It's the same underlying system; you're just telling it which guarantee you want and where.

Try auto-apply in Adaptive Metrics

If you're already using Adaptive Metrics in Grafana Cloud, both versions of auto-apply are available today, no extra setup required. Head to your Adaptive Metrics configuration, pick a segment, and turn it on to see your chosen mode applied on your next recommendation cycle.

For the full mechanics and configuration options, see the auto-apply documentation. It’s worth creating exemptions first for anything you can't afford to lose, and you'll need the Admin role to make the change. 

You can also check your Adaptive Telemetry savings to see the impact on your Grafana Cloud bill.

New to auto-apply? Walk through the full learning journey in our docs: Enable auto-apply in Grafana Adaptive Metrics.

Auto-Apply continuously applies recommendations in either mode with no human intervention, while your existing dashboards, alerts, and queries keep working unchanged.

How cost-first mode decides what to apply

Every recommendation Adaptive Metrics generates comes with a projected change to your series count—some recommendations decrease it, others increase it. Cost-first mode can now take those projected changes into account, much like a careful manual review would, in three steps:

  1. Series-reducing recommendations always apply. Anything that lowers your projected series count goes through immediately, including brand-new recommendations.

  2. Series-increasing recommendations get ranked. Anything that would raise your projected series count is sorted from least impactful to most impactful.

  3. Adaptive Metrics stops at your current total. It works down that ranked list, applying recommendations until the next one would push your projected series count above where it started the cycle.

How coverage-first mode decides what to apply

Coverage-first works more simply than cost-first does: every recommendation gets applied as soon as it's generated, whether it lowers your series count or raises it.

  1. Every recommendation applies, no ranking required. Coverage-first doesn't weigh one recommendation against another or check a budget. It just applies what Adaptive Metrics finds.

  2. Increases go through immediately. If a query comes in for data that's already been aggregated away, the recommendation to restore it at full resolution applies right away, because someone clearly needs that data.

  3. Your metrics stay in lockstep with usage. As what you query shifts week to week, coverage-first adjusts automatically, so nothing you actually use ever falls out of resolution.

The tradeoff is the one cost-first exists to solve: because every increasing recommendation applies too, a spike in queries against previously-aggregated data shows up as a spike in series count.

A simplified example makes this concrete. Say a cycle generates three recommendations:

Recommendation

Effect on series count

Cost-first applied?

Coverage-first applied?

Why

1

-10

Yes

Yes

Decreases series count

2

+5

Yes

Yes

Running total still at or below where it started

3

+10

No

Yes

Would push the running total above where it started

The net effect is that your series count stays flat or drops. It never rises above where you started the cycle, which is the guarantee cost-first mode is built around.

Cost-first vs. coverage-first: when to apply each one

Adaptive Metrics' original auto-apply behavior, coverage-first, maximizes coverage of whatever you're actually querying. It's still there, and it's still the better fit for some of your data. If a dataset is business critical and your team knows exactly what it's querying and why, you want nothing standing between a real query and the raw data behind it. That's the mode we at Grafana Labs use internally for our own critical telemetry.

Cost-first mode is the better fit where cost matters more than guaranteed full coverage. For example, it would be well suited for a PromptQL query that asks for more than the person writing it realized, or an agent issuing queries on your behalf with no visibility into the cost impact downstream. That's increasingly common as less experienced users get access to larger datasets without realizing the potential impact of their queries. In those cases, you'd rather have Adaptive Metrics hold the line on cost and let you review and restore specific data later than have it de-aggregate automatically every time something gets queried unintentionally.

You also don't have to pick one mode for all of your data. Adaptive Metrics' segments feature lets you partition your telemetry along a dimension you choose (e.g., by team, environment, or cluster) and set a different mode on each segment independently. Keep coverage-first on the segments your experts own, and turn on cost-first mode for the segments where cost predictability matters more. It's the same underlying system; you're just telling it which guarantee you want and where.

Try auto-apply in Adaptive Metrics

If you're already using Adaptive Metrics in Grafana Cloud, both versions of auto-apply are available today, no extra setup required. Head to your Adaptive Metrics configuration, pick a segment, and turn it on to see your chosen mode applied on your next recommendation cycle.

For the full mechanics and configuration options, see the auto-apply documentation. It’s worth creating exemptions first for anything you can't afford to lose, and you'll need the Admin role to make the change. 

You can also check your Adaptive Telemetry savings to see the impact on your Grafana Cloud bill.

New to auto-apply? Walk through the full learning journey in our docs: Enable auto-apply in Grafana Adaptive Metrics.

title: Go from alert to post-incident review with Grafana Cloud IRM and AI
summary:
You’ve got 10 minutes before your next meeting when your phone starts ringing. You’re being paged because the frontend is erroring with failed API requests.

You open one tool to see what fired, then another to figure out what’s going on. You message a teammate in Slack to see if they’re noticing the same thing.

That’s a lot of context switching, and it’s still how a lot of teams' incident response works today. Opening another tool and catching someone up takes time. Details can get lost when you manually copy context from one place to another.

It doesn’t have to be this way. With Grafana Cloud IRM, you get on-call support, incident management, chatops in Slack or Microsoft Teams, investigations, and the Grafana mobile app, all connected through the incident record. Let’s follow the frontend incident from the first page through the response and post-incident review to illustrate how your team can start improving their processes today.

The page already has context

When you get paged, you need to understand how serious the problem is and what to check first. With IRM, you’re starting with more than an alert name.

When you open the alert group, it shows the affected service, the dashboard panel tied to the alert, its history, and how many individual alerts were folded into the page.

Imagine the difference between “the frontend is exposing API errors" and “the frontend is exposing HTTP 500 errors from the adService, the issue has already flapped twice in 24 hours, and three related alerts are firing in the same alert group.”

Figuring out what else is affected

Next, you need to figure out whether the frontend errors are isolated or part of something bigger, and whether the platform team is getting paged, too.

A lot of teams will do this by bouncing between dashboards, service maps, observability data, and Slack or Teams.

From the Slack thread, you ask Grafana Assistant, “What else is firing, and how is it related?”

It uses the same alert context you’re looking at and posts the answer back in the same thread.

Click Investigate this alert in the Slack message to get a quick summary of what’s firing and suggestions for what to check next.

Everyone in the thread can see what Assistant found, including teammates who join the response later. If someone has a follow-up, they can ask @Grafana in the thread.

You can ask it to help write a query to check the frontend’s error rate or find the dashboard you need. You can also give Assistant a service-specific playbook through Skills.

Declaring the incident

Once it’s clear this needs a coordinated response, you declare an incident in IRM.

As soon as you do so, IRM handles a number of automated actions for you, removing the need for manual creation every time. You immediately have a dedicated Slack channel, a Zoom call, and an AI investigation that starts looking for the root cause.

You don’t need to worry about the team remembering to create these components. The system does it for you.

Keeping the messy stuff

A lot of the useful information shows up in Slack before anyone knows if it matters.

A teammate remembers a deployment from earlier and suggests it might explain the frontend errors. Someone else has a hypothesis about a dependency. Another person spots something weird on a dashboard.

Usually some of that makes it into the incident record and the rest dies in Slack history.

In IRM, a teammate can react to a Slack message with the robot emoji and drop it onto the incident timeline. The original message, author, and timestamp come with it.

It doesn’t have to be a proven theory. The point is to retain potentially useful context while everyone is still figuring things out.

Managing the incident from Slack

Once the response is underway, the incident commander is juggling roles, tasks, comms, other teams, and the actual investigation.

That can happen in the incident channel without leaving Slack. You can assign roles, create tasks with quick actions, and sync those tasks to Jira or GitHub so they still exist after the incident is closed.

If another team needs to get involved, you can page them from the same place instead of hunting down their on-call schedule. Even better, enter "@Grafana assistant - who is on call?"

The incident owners post status updates that are shared in Slack and pushed to the mobile app so stakeholders can follow along.

An investigation you can actually inspect

The AI investigation starts automatically when you declare the incident.

It takes the context that’s already there (alert data, linked dashboard panels, the timeline, and anything people added from Slack), combines it with your actual data, and starts forming hypotheses about what caused the problem.

The Assistant Workspace feature provides a collaborative environment for you to work alongside the agent and track what it's doing, finding, and thinking. 

You can add a hypothesis, reopen one that got dismissed, mark something disproven, or ask the investigation a question. You can also see the sources behind its conclusions.

A root-cause suggestion is a lot more useful when you can see the evidence, rather than having to decide whether to simply trust a black box. The investigation points to errors from the ad service reaching the frontend as 500 responses. The investigation can also correlate information from outside Grafana through MCP integrations. For example, it checks the earlier deployment hypothesis by checking GitHub directly and finds no evidence linking it to the errors.

It doesn’t matter that it started as a random Slack message. Once it’s in the incident context, it gets evaluated with everything else.

Turning the root cause into the incident record

Once you’ve reviewed the evidence for the leading hypothesis, the findings are added to the incident timeline and shared in Slack as well as pushed to the mobile app. That skips the usual cleanup job of taking what engineering figured out and rewriting it somewhere else so people outside the incident can follow it.

Resolving the incident: mobile app FTW!

You’ve found the root cause with help from the AI investigation and applied a fix to mitigate the issue. You know you still need to write up a post-incident review (PIR), but it’s easy to forget once everyone is back to their normal work.

Thankfully, with the Grafana mobile app, you can keep working from your phone, whether you’re responding to an incident or sorting out your next on-call shift.

So even if you can't get to the PIR immediately and some of the details become fuzzy in your memory, the incident record, timeline, investigation, hypotheses, and sources are all available in the mobile app.

Simply open the investigation on your phone and ask Assistant to create the post-incident review and send it to Confluence. The review is generated from the same history and evidence the team already used during the response. You’re not reconstructing the timeline from memory.

While you’re there, you even check when your next on-call shift starts.

And if you want to see the entire mobile workflow, check out the video below for all the details.

Why this matters

Your team still works in Slack, joins calls, and writes reviews in the tools it already uses. The incident record keeps that work connected. Check out Grafana Cloud IRM today to see how it looks against your own alerts

title: Take Grafana Labs' 5th annual Observability Survey
summary:
Over the past year, "agentic" has gone from an emerging buzzword to an integral part of worklife for many engineers—and that's just scratching the surface on all that's changed. With so much upheaval, there's never been a better time to capture the pulse of the industry, which is why we want you to take Grafana Labs' fifth annual Observability Survey.

We're asking the questions you're probably already arguing about in Slack: Do you trust an agent to ship without review? Are your dashboards still the front door, or has that become a chat window? How many observability tools are too many? And of course, the more things change, the more they stay the same, so we'll continue to track year-over-year trends around cost, tooling, open source, and maturity. 

Available in Brazilian Portuguese, English, Japanese, and Spanish, this is the largest community-driven survey on the state of observability (last year more than 1,350 industry leaders and practitioners participated), and your answers directly shape the free report we'll publish early next year. It also helps you see how you compare to your peers, so please take five to 10 minutes to complete it today.

Enter to win some swag

Of course, it wouldn't be an Observability Survey without the chance to win some cool swag. Every month, we'll randomly select two participants and send them a special Grafana hoodie. And if you see the QR code for the survey at ObservabilityCON, ObservabilityCON on the Road, or a Grafana Labs booth during one of the many events we'll be at between now and Jan. 1, you might even get some special giveaways just for participating. 

And if you don't want to enter to win, that's OK, too. All responses will be kept anonymous; we just want to hear what the community has to say about the state of observability today and where you want it to go in the future.

title: Manage your OpenTelemetry Collectors with Fleet Management in Grafana Cloud
summary:
If you’ve built your telemetry pipelines around OpenTelemetry Collectors, you’ve already invested in a collector distribution, YAML configuration, and a deployment model that fits your infrastructure. As that deployment grows, managing it means keeping shared configuration consistent, accommodating different workloads, and understanding whether your collectors are healthy.

Fleet Management in Grafana Cloud brings those tasks together in one place. With support for the Open Agent Management Protocol (OpAMP) now generally available, you can bring supported OpenTelemetry Collector distributions into Fleet Management while continuing to use the OTel configuration language and components you already know.

We started with Grafana Alloy, Grafana’s distribution of the OpenTelemetry Collector. OpAMP support extends that management workflow to organizations running upstream OTel Collector distributions, so you can adopt centralized management without first migrating to Alloy.

Keep your OTel configuration, manage it across your fleet

For a platform team supporting multiple services or environments, collector configuration often includes both shared policies and workload-specific requirements. You might apply common processing across your fleet while enabling additional collection pipelines only for particular teams, services, or environments.

Fleet Management lets you define those pipelines in OTel YAML and match them to the collectors that should run them. You can update a shared pipeline centrally and apply it across the matching collectors, reducing the work of maintaining configuration separately for each deployment.

For teams using infrastructure as code, Terraform support brings this workflow into your existing processes. You can create pipelines with YAML configuration and register active collectors with Fleet Management, making configuration and enrollment part of a repeatable, version-controlled workflow.

You also get visibility into the collectors running those pipelines. When you enroll an OTel Collector, Fleet Management automatically configures it to send self-monitoring metrics, logs, and traces to Grafana Cloud, regardless of its operating system or deployment mode. For collectors running outside Kubernetes, we also attach a host monitoring pipeline so you can investigate the underlying infrastructure alongside the collector.

These monitoring pipelines remain under your control. Like any other pipeline, you can modify them, turn them off, or send their data to a different backend.

Making OTel configuration work across multiple pipelines

Managing OTel Collectors centrally requires more than accepting YAML. A collector may receive several Fleet Management pipelines alongside its local configuration, and those pieces need to work together as one effective configuration.

This differs from how Alloy handles configuration. Alloy components are defined in blocks and connected by references to their exports. OTel Collectors define components at the top level of the configuration and reference them from one or more telemetry pipelines.

Alloy also keeps local and remote configuration separate. OTel Collectors combine local and remote configuration into one effective configuration. When multiple sources define a component with the same name, one definition can override another, changing how the resulting pipelines behave.

That creates a practical challenge for reusable configuration. Two independently written pipelines might use the same component name, even though each expects that component to behave differently. Teams shouldn’t have to coordinate every component name across all their Fleet Management pipelines to use them together.

To address this, Fleet Management post-processes the remote configuration with a merge algorithm. It adds the Fleet Management pipeline name to OTel pipeline and component identifiers and updates their references accordingly. When multiple sources define components with the same type and configuration, it deduplicates them.

This lets you manage remote pipelines as separate, reusable pieces while Fleet Management handles combining them for the collector. You can organize configuration around what each pipeline does and where it belongs, without manually assembling a separate configuration file for every combination of pipelines.

Use the deployment pattern that fits your infrastructure

Configuration is only one part of managing an OTel deployment. Where you run your collectors, and how telemetry flows, also affects how you apply shared processing and maintain your fleet.

Fleet Management works across collector deployment patterns. For organizations managing a large or mixed fleet, one option worth considering is the gateway pattern.

Separate local collection from shared processing

The gateway pattern separates collection into two layers. Edge collectors gather telemetry from services, pods, and nodes, then send it to gateway collectors. The gateways apply shared processing before forwarding telemetry to a backend.

For example, you might add team labels to metrics, tail-sample traces, or filter logs at the gateway. Keeping these policies in the gateway layer means you can manage shared processing without putting the same logic on every edge collector.

Fleet Management lets you target configuration to each collector’s role: collection pipelines for the edge and shared processing pipelines for the gateways. This gives you a way to manage both layers centrally while keeping their responsibilities distinct.

Introduce OTel gateways into a mixed fleet

Your edge agents and gateways don’t have to use the same software. If you already run software such as Fluent Bit or Telegraf, you can keep those agents at the edge and send telemetry to OTel gateways using compatible protocols.

You can then use Fleet Management to manage the supported OTel gateways and their shared processing configuration. This provides an adoption path for teams that want to introduce OpenTelemetry without replacing every existing agent at once.

The gateway pattern isn’t required for Fleet Management. Whether your collectors send directly to a backend or process telemetry through a gateway layer, OpAMP support lets you bring supported OTel Collectors into a common management workflow.

Bring your OTel fleet into Fleet Management

You can adopt centralized collector management while retaining your OTel distributions, YAML pipelines, and deployment model. Fleet Management brings configuration targeting and collector health into Grafana Cloud, with Terraform support for teams that want to manage the workflow as code.

To get started, enroll an OTel Collector, assign it a YAML pipeline, and view its health. From there, you can extend the same workflow across the collectors and environments you already operate.

title: Manage synthetic checks at scale: Introducing folders in Grafana Cloud Synthetic Monitoring
summary:
As your use of Grafana Cloud Synthetic Monitoring grows, so does the number of checks you need to manage across services, environments, and teams. Eventually, a single flat list of checks becomes difficult to navigate, and even simple questions get harder to answer: Which checks belong to the payments team? Can I disable everything in staging during a maintenance window? Who should be able to edit the checks for this service?

Synthetic Monitoring folders, now generally available, help solve this challenge. You can organize checks into the same Grafana Cloud folders you already use for dashboards and alert rules, making it easier to group checks by team, service, or environment, manage multiple checks at once, and control who can edit them.

The benefits of folders in Synthetic Monitoring

Grafana Cloud Synthetic Monitoring is a black box monitoring solution that lets you proactively assess system reliability and performance by running checks from probe locations around the world. You can set up different types of checks, including ping checks, browser checks, scripted checks, DNS checks, and HTTP checks, to verify system performance at various network levels.

But as your Synthetic Monitoring setup grows, the process of managing checks one at a time doesn’t scale. You could have dozens of checks for the same service, separate sets for production and staging, or hundreds of checks owned by different teams. Without a way to group them, finding the right checks, making changes across them, and keeping ownership clear all require more manual work.

Folders give you a way to manage checks in a way that aligns with how your organization already works. Group checks by team, service, environment, or another structure that makes sense for you, then use that grouping to navigate your checks, take action across them, and control access. Because Synthetic Monitoring uses standard Grafana Cloud folders, the same organizational structure you use for dashboards and alert rules can now extend to your synthetic checks.

Folders bring three key benefits to your Synthetic Monitoring setup:

  • Find the checks you need faster: Browse checks grouped by folder instead of scanning a flat list, and expand only the folders you care about.

  • Manage related checks as a group: Enable, disable, move, or delete every check in a folder in a single operation. This is ideal for managing checks during maintenance windows or environment cleanups.

  • Give teams clearer ownership: Combine Grafana Cloud folder permissions with Synthetic Monitoring roles so each team manages the checks in their own folder.

How folders work

A Synthetic Monitoring check can live in any Grafana Cloud folder you can edit, such as your team's folder, a service folder, or anywhere else in your folder tree. When you create a check in the Synthetic Monitoring app, the default Synthetic Monitoring folder is preselected, and you can change it to any other folder by searching or browsing your folder tree. Checks created without a folder through the API or Terraform are stored in the default folder.

If a folder containing checks is deleted from Grafana Cloud, its checks are automatically moved to the default Synthetic Monitoring folder and keep running without interruption.

Assign checks to folders

When you create or edit a check, use the Folder field to select where it should live. You can also create a new folder right from the check editor.

To organize existing checks, select multiple checks in the check list and use Move to folder to move them all in one operation.

You can also assign checks to folders using the gcx CLI.

Browse and act on groups of checks

The check list offers a folder view in addition to the card and list views. Checks are grouped under their folders, so you can expand only what you need.

From a folder's actions, you can operate on all its checks at once:

  • Enable or disable all checks in the folder (for example, to silence an entire environment during a planned maintenance window).

  • Move all checks to another folder.

  • Delete all checks in the folder.

  • Move the folder itself to another location in your folder tree.

These actions apply to the checks you've selected in the folder or, when nothing is selected, to every check in it, including checks in nested subfolders. Deleting checks never deletes the folder itself.

Manage team access with folder permissions

This is where folders go beyond organization. Folder permissions work together with Synthetic Monitoring roles, so you can control which folders each user or team can manage. For example, the payments team could have edit permissions on the payments folder, while everyone else in the org only gets view access.

For more information on how to set up access permissions, refer to our documentation.

Provision folders as code

If you manage your synthetic checks through automation, folders are supported there, too. Options include:

  • Synthetic Monitoring API: checks accept a folderUid field on create and update.

  • Terraform: the grafana_synthetic_monitoring_check resource accepts a folder_uid attribute (Grafana Terraform provider v4.37.0 or later). Terraform remains the source of truth for the checks it manages: if someone moves a Terraform-managed check to a different folder in the UI, the next terraform plan reports the change as drift, and applying moves the check back to the folder defined in your configuration (or to the default folder, if none is set).

Wrapping up

Folders make it easier to scale your Synthetic Monitoring setup, giving you a consistent way to organize and manage checks. And because folders work across the UI, API, and Terraform, you can bring that same structure to both manual and automated workflows.

To learn more and get started, refer to our documentation for organizing checks in folders.
